titleStmt.title: Global Versus Local Schedulability Analysis of a Two-Level Hierarchical System

analytic.title: Global Versus Local Schedulability Analysis of a Two-Level Hierarchical System

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Aircraft systems manage resource sharing among several uniprocessor modules operating under the ARINC 653 specification. This standard, based on a two-level hierarchical architecture, guarantees function isolation within partitions. Partitions are scheduled on the processor according to an infinitely repeated offline statically defined cycle. During each cycle, a partition may be accessed either once or multiple times. This study focuses on the case where each partition is granted a single processor access per cycle.

We propose an approach that involves transforming a twolevel hierarchical scheduling model into a conventional uni-level system. This transformation enables the application of existing results from non-hierarchical uniprocessor scheduling for analysis. We establish a correlation between the schedulability properties of both systems and derive an exact schedulability criterion for fully harmonic task sets. Additionally, we extend this approach to compute precise worst-case response times of tasks within a two-level hierarchical system, leveraging established uniprocessor schedulability results. Finally, we evaluate the scalability of this method.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The increasing complexity of embedded systems has led to a substantial rise in data exchange between functions, necessitating new computational models based on resource sharing. Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA) is one such model, comprising uniprocessor computational modules that adhere to the ARINC 653 standard. These modules are interconnected via network links conforming to the Ethernet-based ARINC 664 standard (AFDX). In IMA architectures, avionics functions are distributed across multiple modules to enhance system resilience, flexibility, and computational efficiency. This study focuses on a single computational module operating under the ARINC 653 standard.

In ARINC 653-based hierarchical systems, each partition is assigned a specific criticality level. Functions are defined as a set of tasks, which are grouped into partitions based on their criticality level. A task can execute only when the processor is allocated to its partition. The scheduling is thus performed at two different levels:
(i) system level: scheduling of partitions on the processor;

(ii) partition level: scheduling of tasks within their partition. Depending on the processor's scheduling, a partition may be granted processor access either once (uni-access) or multiple times (multi-access) within a periodic cycle. In this paper, we focus on the uni-access problem.

The parameters of embedded tasks (e.g., execution times, periods, deadlines, . . . ), are specified by the system designer at the system level, without consideration of the underlying twolevel architecture. However, for certification purposes, it is essential to demonstrate compliance with all timing constraints, particularly deadlines. Therefore, both scheduling levels must be accounted for when verifying these constraints. Partition scheduling follows a statically defined periodic cycle. Within each partition (partition level), tasks can be scheduled using various policies, such as Rate Monotonic (RM) or Earliest Deadline First (EDF). In this paper, we consider tasks with implicit deadlines (where each task's deadline is equal to its period) scheduled with RM at partitions level.

This two-level hierarchical scheduling problem has already been studied in the literature. However, we propose a novel approach, which aims at simplifying the analysis through the use of well-known classical uni-processor scheduling analysis. We will specifically focus on schedulability criteria and worst response time calculation. The core principle relies on two clocks: a global system clock, corresponding to the wall-clock and a local clock that is specific to each partition, which only runs when the partition has access to the processor. The supply function sf A maps any global time instant t to the corresponding local time t local for a given partition A.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III introduces the system model, the notations, and the problem statement. Our main contribution, which purpose is to convert a hierarchical architecture into a local uni-processor system, is detailed in Section IV. We use this to analyze the schedulability of a set of fully harmonic task. In Section V, we describe an algorithm for computing the worst-case response time (WCRT) of tasks in hierarchical systems, and we illustrate the special case of tasks with periods that are multiples of the cycle period. An evaluation proving the scalability of our approach is presented in Section VI. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper with remarks and perspectives for future work. based on their period (the lower the period, the higher the priority). The scheduling of periodic task sets using RM has been extensively studied in the context of uniprocessor systems. Numerous studies have explored schedulability under RM. In the case of implicit deadlines (the relative deadline of a task equals its period), Liu and Layland proposed a sufficient condition, based on the utilization factor [14], while a tighter sufficient condition, known as the hyperbolic bound, was introduced by Bini et al. [6], [7].

An alternative approach to schedulability analysis consists in comparing task response times to their relative deadlines. Joseph and Pandya developed an algorithm for calculating the exact worst-case response time for independent, periodic tasks scheduled under Rate Monotonic (RM) [10]. It was generalized by Lehoczky for non-implicit deadlines in [12].

Tindell introduced a new parameter for periodic tasks, known as the offset [24]. This parameter modifies the initial release time of a task, potentially reducing the response time of each task within the system by staggering their execution over time.

The aforementioned works only considered traditional uniprocessor architectures, where the processor is fully dedicated to the execution of a set of tasks. We now focus on results obtained in the context of hierarchical architectures.

Mok, Feng, and Chen defined two models of partitions for hierarchical scheduling [16], which involve either static or dynamic partition scheduling. In our work, we focus on their static model. One of the primary areas of interest concerns the determination of the parameters of the partition. For instance, Lipari and Bini [13] computed partition parameters based on the assigned tasks to optimize partitioning. A holistic optimization approach was proposed by Yoon et al. , that facilitates the determination of partition parameters [25]. In this paper, we focus on the schedulability of tasks, assuming that the partition scheduling has already been performed.

Mok et al. introduced a response time analysis for static partitions with multi-access [16]. However, it is important to note that their analysis is primarily theoretical, as the supply function is not explicitly defined. For partitions with uniaccess, Shin and Lee [20] [21] provided the supply function. Almeida and Pedreiras analyzed the periodic server model, using the server availability function [1] for tasks with jitter. In the same paper, they proposed a heuristic algorithm for designing server parameters. Davis and Burns [8] examined the response time of tasks within different types of servers, including sporadic and deferrable servers, improving prior work of Saewong et al. [19].

Palencia et al. proposed an alternative method, related to the offset task model [17]. In this approach, each interval during which the partition is not allowed to access the processor is represented by a periodic virtual task with offset. These fictive tasks introduce interference with the tasks under analysis.

Other studies have explored hierarchical scheduling without relying on response time analysis algorithms. [22]. Fu et al. also used model checking through the theory of priced timed automata [9]. In this approach, the schedulability condition is expressed as a set of temporal logic expressions and verified using a model checker.

Our algorithm for computing the response times of periodic tasks in a hierarchical system is based on the multiframe task model, as defined by Mok and Chen [15] and later generalized by Baruah et al. [3]. In this model, tasks are composed of instances, or frames, each with distinct parameters, such as deadlines or execution times. Baruah et al. [4] also presented a response time analysis for tasks following this model.

An alternative approach would involve using the transaction model of Tindell [24]. Both models can be analyzed in an equivalent manner: Rahni et al. [18] compared the generalized multiframe (GMF) model and the transaction model, showing that the methods proposed for the transaction model can be applied to analyze the schedulability of GMF task sets [4].

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL AND PROBLEM STATEMENT
div.p: Hereafter, we present our model for systems with two-level hierarchical scheduling.

div.head: A. Task model
div.p: We analyze the schedulability of a set Γ of independent, and periodic tasks. A periodic task is executed on a recurring basis. An execution is referred to as a job or task instance. Each task τ i is characterized by the following parameters:

• C i : the worst-case execution time (WCET) of the task; • T i : the period of the task, which is the exact duration between the releases of two consecutive jobs; • D i : the relative deadline of the task, which defines the time window within which each job should be completed, starting from its release time. The k-th job of a periodic task τ i is released at time r i,k = r i +(k -1)T i , where r i is the first release of the task. Each job has an absolute deadline d i,k = r i + kD i . If r i is known, the task is said to be concrete and is defined by (r i , C i , T i , D i ). Otherwise, the task is non-concrete and is defined by the tuple
div.formula: (C i , T i , D i )
div.p: The utilization factor represents the proportion of processor time allocated to the execution of the task set. Non-concrete tasks with implicit deadlines (D i = T i) are fully described by τ i = (C i , T i ), and we have:
div.formula: d i,k = r i +kT i .
div.p: During execution, tasks compete to access the processor. Depending on when jobs are activated, the competition can be more or less exacerbated. As a result, the response time of jobs, i.e., the time between their activation and their completion, varies depending on the release scenario. To analyze the schedulability of a task set, a necessary and sufficient condition exists: it consists of computing the worst-case response time of each task and checking that this time is less than or equal to their relative deadline.

Definition 2. The worst-case response time (WCRT) of a task τ i , denoted R i , is defined as the maximum duration between the release and the completion of any of its jobs. It represents the longest time a job of τ i may take to execute, from its activation until its completion. Definition 3. A task set Γ is schedulable by a given scheduling policy if, for all tasks τ i ∈ Γ, the worst-case response time R i satisfies the condition R i ≤ D i .

Classically, for RM, a simultaneous release of a task set (for example for all i, r i = 0) is known to result in the worstcase response time (WCRT). This result no longer holds in a hierarchical architecture due to the scheduling of partitions. Thus, we will have to determine the new conditions of a worst case scenario within these constraints.

div.head: B. Execution model
div.p: A computational module is modeled as a two-level hierarchical uniprocessor system. At system level, the processor time is shared between m partitions, denoted A 1 , . . . , A m , where m ∈ N * . Our work is based on the static partition model developed by Mok et al. [16]. The scheduling of partitions is defined off-line as a periodic cycle of length T cyc , which is infinitely repeated.

Without loss of generality, and for the sake of clarity, the partition under consideration will be denoted as A. It is associated with a set of tasks Γ A . In this paper, we assume that partition A is granted access to the processor during a single contiguous time window per cycle, referred to as the Access Time Interval (ATI), denoted (S A , E A ]. S A and E A represent the start and end times of this interval relatively to the beginning of the system level cycle. During the remainder of the cycle, the partition is suspended and does not have access to the processor.

For the partition A, a local clock counts the cumulative time allocated to A when the partition is active. This clock runs only during the corresponding ATI, whereas the global clock never stops. The supply function establishes the link between the global clock and the local clock. It will be explicitly defined in Section III.C.

div.head: C. Supply function
div.p: The supply function was first defined by Mok et al. [16] and completed by Shin and Lee [20]. The supply function sf A of a partition A associates to each t (t ≥ 0), the total amount of processor time allocated to the partition A during the global time interval [0, t).

Mok et al. proved in [16] that, in the case of RM scheduling, the critical instant for the task set of partition A necessarily occurs at the end of an ATI. To simplify future equations and without loss of generality, the origin of the cycle can be set by construction so that the ATI is located at the end of the cycle. Therefore, we have: E A = T cyc . This is made possible for two reasons: firstly, the partition scheduling is statically defined, forming an infinitely repeating cycle; and secondly, tasks are non-concrete, with no constraint on their release times.

The outline of the schedulability analysis is depicted in Fig. 6:

• The parameters of each task τ i = (C i , T i ), defined at the system level according to the global clock, are used to determine the corresponding local parameters (in the unilevel system) within the partition as a GMF model, using the supply function; • Then, uni-level scheduling results are used to obtain schedulability conditions or WCRT; • Finally, the computed WCRT R A i is converted to global WCRT R i , using the inverse supply function.

In the GMF model [3] [4] (further described in Section IV), a task consists of multiple frames (instances), each characterized by distinct parameters. In our case, we assume that while each frame maintains the same WCET, the interval between its release and its deadline may vary. Given that the tasks have implicit deadlines, a GMF task can be described by two parameters: its WCET and a vector of relative deadlines (one relative deadline per frame).

In the next section, we show how global task parameters can be converted into local task parameters, using the supply function. We also prove the equivalence between local and global exact worst-case response time analysis.

div.head: IV. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section, we first define the scenario leading to the worst-case response time (Section IV-A). Then (Section IV-B), we introduce the local model of tasks that we use. Then we use classical uni-level scheduling results. Next, we show for the global system (Section IV-C) how the schedulability analysis and the WCRT can be deduced from our local analysis. Finally, special attention is paid to the case of fully harmonic tasks (Section IV-D).

div.head: A. Worst-case scenario
div.p: The results presented in this section are applicable to any work-conserving scheduling algorithm used within partitions, provided it is based on fixed priorities (thus including RM). Definition 4. A scheduling algorithm is said to be workconserving, if it does not leave the processor idle as long as there are pending tasks.

Definition 5. Considering a task τ i , a level-i busy period [12] is an interval between two consecutive level-i idle times. A level-i idle time corresponds to a time, where all the previously released tasks with priority higher than or equal to the priority of τ i have been completed.

We now define, in the local system, the scenario leading to the worst-case response time for a task in the global system. Defining a scenario consists of defining the release times of all the tasks. Theorem 1. If a fixed-priority and work-conserving scheduling algorithm is used in partition A, the worst-case response time R i for a task τ i ∈ Γ A is obtained, when all the tasks from Γ A are simultaneously released at t global = 0 (and then t local = 0).

Proof. In order to determine the worst-case response time for a task τ i in the global system, we define its critical instant [2], [5], [14]. This instant is a level-i idle time at the beginning of its longest busy period. By definition, the duration of this busy period represents the worst-case response time because the execution of τ i ends, in the worst-case, at the end of the busy period.

Using fixed priority algorithm, the critical instant of a task τ i occurs when it is released simultaneously (generally at time 0) with all the higher priority tasks [2], [5], [14]. Considering the sf A function, simultaneous release in the global system corresponds to simultaneous release in the local system.

By definition of isf A , the worst case response time for the task τ i in the global system happens, when it is released at the end of an ATI, i.e, at a time E A + kT cyc (with k ∈ N). Since we have E A = T cyc , this maximum waiting time is obtained at any kT cyc . Time 0 in global time can thus be chosen as the critical instant. We have sf A (0) = 0, hence the result.

For the remainder of the paper, we now assume that all tasks are simultaneously released at time 0 in both the local and global systems. We examine the worst-case scenario and then determine schedulability criteria or the response-time under this hypothesis.

div.head: C. Local and global schedulability
div.p: In this section, we explain how our local system can be used to address the two-level hierarchical schedulability problem. Specifically, we establish a link between the global WCRT and local WCRT, thereby deducing an equivalence between the schedulability of our local system and that of the overall system.

div.head: D. Schedulability analysis for fully harmonic task sets
div.p: In this section, we illustrate the use of Th. 4 to propose a schedulability condition, based on the utilisation factor of a partition in the case of fully harmonic task sets. Definition 6. A task set Γ is harmonic if, for every couple (τ i , τ j ) from Γ, either T i is a multiple of T j or conversely. Definition 7. A task set Γ is fully harmonic if the task set is harmonic and if all the periods are multiples of T cyc .

We first prove that local tasks remain periodic for fully harmonic task sets using Th. 2. Proposition 1. If the period of a periodic task τ i of a partition A is multiple of T cyc , then the associated local task is periodic, with a period equal to U A T i .
Proof. Let τ i be a periodic task where T i is a multiple of T cyc , we have:
div.formula: N A i = lcm(T cyc , T i ) T i = T i T i = 1
div.p: Since N A i = 1, the relative deadlines of the local GMF task are described by 1-ary vector. It is thus periodic and its parameters are (C i , T A i = sf A (T i ) = T i .U A ). Furthermore, we prove that a fully harmonic task set remains locally harmonic.
Corollary 1. If a task set Γ A of a partition A is fully harmonic then the associated local tasks are periodic and harmonic.

Proof. Since for each task τ i ∈ Γ, T i is a multiple of T cyc , each local task remains periodic (Prop. 1). Since the tasks are harmonic, let us consider two tasks τ i and τ j , such that T i is a multiple of T j . Then T i .U A is also a multiple of T j .U A . The set of the local tasks is thus harmonic. Now, when the tasks are harmonic, the scheduling order under RM is identical to that under EDF [11]. Under EDF, the schedulability criterion U ≤ 1 is exact. Thus we can use it to find a schedulability criterion for fully harmonic task set in a hierarchical architecture framework. Theorem 5. A task set Γ A fully harmonic is schedulable by RM if and only if:

div.p: Thus the task set is locally schedulable if and only if the local utilization factor is less than or equal to U A . Besides, using theorem Th. 4, a task is globally schedulable if and only if the task is locally schedulable. Thus, the task set is globally schedulable if and only if the local utilization factor is less than or equal to U A .

div.head: V. RESPONSE-TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section, we introduce a novel approach for determining the worst-case response time of non-concrete tasks within a two-level hierarchical scheduling framework. As previously outlined, we leverage the supply function to transform the hierarchical scheduling problem into that of classical uniprocessor real-time scheduling. The resulting set of tasks is represented as a set of generalized multiframes (GMF). Then, we are able to derive the Worst-Case Response Times, building on existing non-hierarchical uniprocessor results from the literature.

As proved by Th. 2, a periodic task on a two-level hierarchical architecture can be turned into a generalized multiframe task, when scheduled at the partition level. In order to compute the exact WCRT of a set of generalized multiframes on a uniprocessor system under RM scheduling, it is recalled that the critical instant for any task occurs whenever the task is released simultaneously with all higher priority tasks.

A response-time analysis can be simplified by treating local tasks as strictly periodic rather than GMF tasks. The period assigned to a task τ A i is taken as min(D A i,k ). This approach represents the limiting case of the GMF model, resulting in a conservative analysis that may overestimates the worst-case response time, thus leading to a non-exact evaluation.

Rahni et al. [18] proposed translating the GMF model into the transaction model. Tindell [24] introduced the transaction model based on offsets as an extension of the Liu & Layland task model. In this model, transactions are non-concrete, and the offset is defined as the time delay experienced by the first job of a periodic task.

The authors demonstrated that the transaction scheduling analysis techniques can be applied to the GMF tasks. They derived an approach for calculating the exact WCRT of generalized multiframe tasks. However, their approach suffered from combinatorial explosion problems. Indeed, as Takada and Sakamura [23] showed, since the characteristics of jobs from the same task can vary, it is necessary to examine all possible combinations of simultaneous arrivals for the instances of all tasks.

However, in our model, it has been demonstrated, that the critical instant corresponds to the simultaneous activation of the first instance of each task at instant 0. Therefore, there is only one possible combination, where the first instances of each generalized multiframe are activated simultaneously at time 0. The following theorem is an application of the work of [18], with a single scenario being analyzed. Theorem 6. Let τ i be a non-concrete task running on a twolevel hierarchical system and τ A i its local associated GMF task model, according to Th. 2. Let hp A i denote the set of local GMF tasks with higher priority than τ A i . The exact WCRT of τ i is equal to: R i = isf A (R A i ) where R A i , the exact local WCRT, is the result of the fixed-point equation:

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: This paper analyzed task scheduling in hierarchical systems based on the uni-access periodic partition model by Mok et al. [16]. A novel approach was introduced, linking periodic global tasks to local GMF tasks to address this scheduling challenge. The objective was to leverage the rich legacy of uniprocessor schedulability theory. A local model has been proposed to achieve this objective. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this model through the development of an exact schedulability criterion for fully harmonic task sets and a pseudo-polynomial algorithm for response-time analysis applicable to non-fully harmonic task sets. Furthermore, we showed that the analysis can be simplified when all task periods are multiples of the cycle period.

Future work will extend this research to hierarchical systems with multi-access partitions. We plan to define a general supply function, reusing our local framework, to compute the WCRT of tasks in the context of multiple access. To the best of our knowledge and available bibliography, hierarchical schedulabilty analysis is currently hindered by its high computational costs. In a naive approach, the WCRT of each task has to be computed for every potential critical instant (growing with the number of processor access windows per cycle). The methodology presented in this paper is thus foundational work, as we aim, with our framework, to minimize the number of critical instants to test for each task, enabling faster computation of the exact WCRT.

div.head: VI. EVALUATIONS
div.p: This section presents an evaluation of the execution time of our response-time analysis algorithm, verifying its scalability in real-world applications. First, we introduce the parameters used to generate multiple systems for simulation. Next, we analyze the algorithm's execution time, studying the influence of various generation parameters. All evaluations were conducted using a C++ program executed on an Intel®Core™i5-10505 CPU@3.20GHz×12 processor.

div.head: A. System generation
div.p: A system in our simulation is defined as a uni-access partition containing a task set. The system is generated using the following parameters:
• the cycle period T cyc ;
• the utilization factor of the partition U A ;

• the utilization factor of the task set within the partition U ; • the number of task n A . The ATI parameters are derived directly from T cyc and U A . The task set is generated by allocating portions of U to each task such that the sum of individual utilizations U i equals U . Each task's period is randomly selected under the condition T i ≥ T cyc and the WCET is subsequently determined based on T i and U i .

div.head: B. Analysis of the execution time
div.p: To conduct our simulation, we generated multiple systems. In an initial configuration, we fix parameters as: T cyc = 500, U A = 0.2, U = 0.5 and n A = 20. Under these conditions, the execution time to compute response times for all tasks within the partition are approximately 2 ms. This finding substantiates the scalability of the algorithm, as system verification remains within the order of seconds or minutes even as the number of partitions increases.

Then, we evaluate the influence of the generation parameters on the execution time of our program. In Fig. 10 and Fig. 11, we respectively vary U A and U for different number of tasks: n A ∈ {5, 20, 35, 50} while keeping the other parameters constant. Each average execution time is computed over 500 system generations. Fig. 10 illustrates that the partition utilization factor does not affect the average execution time.
